profile.reading:
The Cox Data Center sits in unincorporated north Fulton County, Georgia, in the Roswell-Alpharetta corridor a short drive from Cox Enterprises' Atlanta headquarters. It is tagged in mapping data simply as a data center building, with no public address, floor plan, or capacity figures attached to it -- a pattern common to facilities a company builds and runs purely for its own network rather than to lease out to others.

Cox Communications is the cable, broadband, and telephone subsidiary of Cox Enterprises, a privately held, family-controlled media and communications company founded in Atlanta and still headquartered there. Cox delivers video, internet, and phone service to millions of residential and business customers over its own hybrid fiber-coaxial and fiber-to-the-home network across roughly 18 states. A facility built inside Cox's home market fits the profile of a regional headend or network hub: the building where a cable operator terminates its fiber backbone, houses the electronics that originate video and internet service, and connects out to the neighborhood plant serving Roswell, Alpharetta, and the rest of north Fulton County -- a different function from a leased colocation data center, which helps explain why nothing about this building is marketed publicly.

That absence of detail is not particular to this site. Cox Business, the company's commercial colocation product, advertises 21 locations across its footprint built to Tier III standards with HIPAA, SOC 2, and PCI compliance -- including one in Macon, Georgia. Metro Atlanta, Cox's home market and by far its largest concentration of subscribers, is conspicuously absent from that list, a strong signal that this Fulton County facility is not part of Cox's for-lease colocation business at all, but internal infrastructure supporting its own subscriber network. Separately, cable operators' own filings with the Federal Communications Commission make a related practice explicit: in Cox's cable system profiles filed with the FCC, headend and technical facility address details are described as "retained in local files" rather than disclosed publicly. An operator can be required to tell a regulator where its plant is without that information ever becoming public record.

No public announcement, permit filing, or trade-press coverage specific to this address turned up in research for this record. What can be said with reasonable confidence is what the building's role most likely is, and why: as a piece of Cox's own network infrastructure rather than a commercial product, it was never built to be found by the public in the first place.

reading.body:
This facility's published specifications contain no power capacity, IT load, cooling, or technical detail of any kind. The operator has not disclosed the megawatt demand or rack count that would indicate whether this campus contributes materially to AI infrastructure in the state.

Georgia has 33 mapped data centers, but only four publish power capacity figures to the public. Those four facilities total 66.3 megawatts of disclosed capacity. This Cox facility ranks fifth among Georgia sites, which means it does not appear in the published four, so no figure can be assigned to it from operator disclosure.

Without published watts, racks, or power density from Cox Communications, this campus cannot be read as a constraint on AI scaling or as a meaningful point of reference for grid demand in the state. The operator's choice not to publish specifications means this facility is not a legible node in the infrastructure that bounds AI compute capacity.
